You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
# Clinical Vignette: Marco R.

Marco R. was fifty-three when the police stopped him on a Tuesday evening in late October, three years ago. He had been driving home from his office in downtown Miami after a long day of reconciling corporate tax filings—work that usually steadied him, gave him something concrete to hold. The officer who approached his window was young, maybe twenty-five, with his hand already moving toward his belt. Marco, who had grown up in this city, whose parents had come from Puerto Rico with nothing, knew the script. He kept his hands visible. He spoke softly. He did everything right.

The beating came anyway. It came fast and without warning, as though his compliance had been irrelevant from the start. The officer's partner joined in. Marco remembered the sound of his own ribs cracking, the taste of blood, the way his vision narrowed to a single point of light before everything went dark. When he woke in the hospital, his left arm was fractured in two places. The stitches across his cheekbone would leave a scar that he still touches sometimes, as if checking that it is still there. The official report said he had "resisted." The charges were eventually dropped. No one was disciplined.

For the first weeks afterward, Marco functioned. He returned to work after six weeks, moving carefully through the office in a way his colleagues pretended not to notice. But by November, something had shifted in how he moved through the world. He began avoiding the routes he used to take to the office, steering away from any street where he had seen a police car. He stopped going to the grocery store on Saturday mornings when it was crowded; the thought of being in an unfamiliar place where he could not quickly assess who was around, where he could not see the exits clearly, made his chest tighten. Each time he spotted a patrol car or found himself in a crowded space, the same thought arrived with certainty: he was marked, visible in a way that made him a target. The fear was not abstract—it was a logic that felt airtight, confirmed by what had already happened to him. He could not explain this to himself in language that made sense—only that he needed to know where danger might come from before he entered a space. He began identifying escape routes in every room he entered, tracing them mentally the way other men might scan a menu. At the gym, he positioned himself near the door. At client meetings, he sat where he could see the hallway.

What frightened Marco most, though, was not the fear itself but what the fear meant about him. He had come to believe that something intrinsic to him—something in his bearing, his skin, his very presence—had invited that violence. If he had been someone else, someone less marked by his own history, perhaps the officer would have seen a man instead of a threat. This thought, once it took hold, would not release him. When he caught his reflection unexpectedly, he would see the scar and feel a surge of shame so acute it nearly stopped his breath. He began to isolate himself, declining invitations from colleagues, letting his friendships attenuate into polite text messages that grew further apart. His ex-wife called once to check on him; he did not call back. He had come to feel set apart from other people in a way he could not bridge, as though the trauma had marked him as fundamentally different, fundamentally wrong.

The isolation deepened his hypervigilance. With fewer people in his life to anchor him to normalcy, Marco's mind had more room to work. He scrolled through news reports of police shootings, each one landing like a confirmation of his own vulnerability. When he saw footage of an injured person—a man with a bandaged face, a woman with visible bruising—something in his nervous system would spike. These images told him something he was already certain of: that violence was random, that he could not predict or prevent it, and that his skin and his history had made him a permanent target. Each injury he witnessed became another piece of evidence that the world was designed to hurt men like him. The image would pull him back into that Tuesday evening, and he would feel the phantom pain in his ribs, the pressure in his chest. These moments of contact with others' injuries, with reminders of victimization, would send him spiraling into deeper conviction that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that he was fundamentally unable to protect himself. The checking behind him intensified. The mental mapping of exits became obsessive. He began sleeping with his bedroom door locked and a flashlight on the nightstand.

By the time Marco came to his first session three months ago, his work had begun to suffer. He had missed two important client meetings, citing illness. His supervisor had started asking questions. He sat in the office with his shoulders pulled tight, his eyes tracking the window, and said quietly that he did not know how much longer he could do this—not the work, not any of it. He was not sure his life was worth living anymore, and he meant it in a way that frightened him. What he wanted most was to feel safe again, to trust that he could walk into a room without mapping every exit, to look at another person's scar without feeling his own wounds reopen.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette establishes triggers (patrol cars, crowded spaces, images of injured people) and negative appraisals ('he was marked, visible in a way that made him a target'; 'something intrinsic to him had invited that violence'; 'fundamentally wrong'), but no paragraph conveys a direct causal relationship between encountering triggers and the formation or intensification of these negative appraisals. The negative beliefs appear to develop from the trauma itself and are confirmed by evidence-seeking, but the vignette does not explicitly show triggers driving the appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

But by November, something had shifted in how he moved through the world. He began avoiding the routes he used to take to the office, steering away from any street where he had seen a police car. He stopped going to the grocery store on Saturday mornings when it was crowded; the thought of being in an unfamiliar place where he could not quickly assess who was around, where he could not see the exits clearly, made his chest tighten. Each time he spotted a patrol car or found himself in a crowded space, the same thought arrived with certainty: he was marked, visible in a way that made him a target.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Every patrol car he glimpsed seemed to confirm what he was already beginning to suspect—that he was exposed, that his presence alone could provoke violence. Crowded spaces where he could not see exits made him feel trapped, and this helplessness fed a deeper conviction: he was not like other men; something about him invited threat.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He began to isolate himself, declining invitations from colleagues, letting his friendships attenuate into polite text messages that grew further apart. His ex-wife called once to check on him; he did not call back. He had come to feel set apart from other people in a way he could not bridge, as though the trauma had marked him as fundamentally different, fundamentally wrong.

The isolation deepened his hypervigilance. With fewer people in his life to anchor him to normalcy, Marco's mind had more room to work. He scrolled through news reports of police shootings, each one landing like a confirmation of his own vulnerability. When he saw footage of an injured person—a man with a bandaged face, a woman with visible bruising—something in his nervous system would spike.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each image of another man's injuries, each news report of violence against someone who looked like him, seemed to whisper the same message: this is what the world does to people like you. The footage did not merely distress him; it crystallized his belief that his skin, his history, his very presence had made him a permanent mark.
<<<END>>>
